The New England Journal of Medicine (2011) published a study analyzing the outcomes of HIV treatment, specifically focusing on the initiation of highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) and its impact on patient health. 2. Ahdieh-Grant et al. (2003) conducted a cohort study to determine the optimal timing for initiating HAART in HIV-infected individuals, as published in the American Journal of Epidemiology. 3. Althoff et al. (2010) examined the virologic and immunologic responses to HAART across different age groups and regimen classes, with findings published in AIDS. 4. The ART Cohort Collaboration (2003) highlighted the prognostic importance of the initial response to potent antiretroviral therapy in HIV-1-infected patients, as detailed in The Lancet. 5. Another study by the ART Cohort Collaboration (2009) explored the clinical significance of baseline CD4 cell counts on short-term immunologic responses to ART in individuals with virologic suppression, published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes. 6. The CASCADE Collaboration (2011) investigated the timing of HAART initiation and its effects on clinical outcomes in HIV-1 seroconverters, as reported in the Archives of Internal Medicine. 7. A separate CASCADE Collaboration study (2003) analyzed short-term CD4 cell responses after HAART initiation at various times post-seroconversion in 1,500 seroconverters, published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes. 8. Cozzi-Lepri et al. (2001) provided evidence from the ICONA study on when to start HAART in chronically HIV-infected patients, as published in AIDS. 9. Egger et al. (2002) conducted a collaborative analysis of prospective studies to assess the prognosis of HIV-1-infected patients starting HAART, with results published in The Lancet. 10. Garcia et al. (2004) examined the long-term CD4+ T-cell response to HAART based on baseline CD4+ T-cell counts, as detailed in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes. 11. Gras et al. (2007) demonstrated that achieving CD4 cell counts of 800 cells/mm³ or greater after seven years of HAART is feasible for most patients starting with 350 cells/mm³ or higher, as published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes. 12. The HIV-CAUSAL Collaboration (2010) assessed the effect of combined antiretroviral therapy on overall mortality in HIV-infected individuals, as reported in AIDS. 13. Another study by the HIV-CAUSAL Collaboration (2011) evaluated the timing of combined antiretroviral therapy initiation to reduce mortality and AIDS-defining illnesses in developed countries, published in the Annals of Internal Medicine. 14. Kitahata et al. (2009) compared the effects of early versus deferred antiretroviral therapy on survival in HIV-infected individuals, as detailed in the New England Journal of Medicine. 15. Krishnan et al. (2011) analyzed the incidence of non-AIDS-defining cancers in antiretroviral treatment-naïve subjects after initiating ART, with findings published in Oncology. 16. Merito and Pezzotti (2006) compared the costs and effectiveness of different starting points for HAART in HIV-positive patients, as reported in the European Journal of Health Economics. 17. Opravil et al. (2002) evaluated the clinical efficacy of early HAART initiation in asymptomatic HIV-infected patients with CD4 cell counts >350 cells/μL, as published in AIDS. 18. Palella et al. (2003) assessed the survival benefits of initiating ART in HIV-infected individuals across different CD4+ cell strata, as detailed in the Annals of Internal Medicine. 19. Phillips et al. (2001) examined the HIV viral load response to ART based on baseline CD4 cell counts and viral load, as published in JAMA. 20. Plettenberg et al. (2011) analyzed the impact of earlier HAART initiation on immune status and clinical outcomes in treated patients, based on cohort data from the German Competence Network for HIV/AIDS, as reported in Infection. 21. Gallant et al. (2007) investigated health outcomes associated with the timing of ART initiation, with findings accessible online. 22. The When to Start Consortium (2009) conducted a collaborative analysis of 18 HIV cohort studies to determine the optimal timing for ART initiation in AIDS-free HIV-1-infected patients, as published in The Lancet. 23. Grant et al. (2013) explored the association of baseline viral load, CD4 count, and week 4 virologic response with virologic failure in ACTG Study A5202, with findings available online. 24. Suthar et al. (2012) conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on the use of ART for tuberculosis prevention in adults with HIV, as published in PLoS Medicine. 25. Golub et al. (2007) examined the impact of ART and isoniazid preventive therapy on tuberculosis incidence in HIV-infected patients in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, as reported in AIDS. 26. Badri et al. (2002) studied the effect of HAART on tuberculosis incidence in South Africa, as detailed in The Lancet. 27. Golub et al. (2008) analyzed recurrent tuberculosis in HIV-infected patients in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, as published in AIDS. 28. Williams et al. (2010) assessed the role of ART in tuberculosis control across nine African countries, as reported in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. 29. Donnell et al. (2011) evaluated heterosexual HIV-1 transmission after ART initiation in a prospective cohort analysis, as published in The Lancet. 30. The Antiretroviral Pregnancy Registry Steering Committee provided data on the use of ART during pregnancy to prevent mother-to-child transmission of HIV, with findings accessible online. 31. Akinbami et al. (2012) analyzed CD4 count patterns and demographic distribution in treatment-naïve HIV patients in Lagos, Nigeria, as reported in AIDS Research and Treatment. 32. Abdool Karim et al. (2011) studied the integration of ART with tuberculosis treatment, as detailed in the New England Journal of Medicine. 33. Havlir et al. (2011) examined the timing of ART initiation for HIV-1 infection and tuberculosis, as published in the New England Journal of Medicine. 34. Blanc et al. (2011) compared earlier versus later ART initiation in HIV-infected adults with tuberculosis, as reported in the New England Journal of Medicine. 35. Hoffmann et al. (2009) analyzed the long-term outcomes of hepatitis B and HIV co-infection in HAART recipients, as published in AIDS. 36. Thio et al. (2002) assessed the risk of liver-related mortality in HIV-1 and hepatitis B virus co-infected individuals, as reported in The Lancet. 37. Konopnicki et al. (2005) studied the prevalence and impact of hepatitis B on AIDS progression and mortality in the EuroSIDA cohort, as published in AIDS. 38. Puoti et al. (2000) examined liver disease-related mortality in HIV-infected patients, as detailed in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes. 39. Weber et al. (2006) analyzed liver-related deaths in HIV-infected individuals in the D:A:D study, as reported in the Archives of Internal Medicine. 40. Salmon-Ceron et al. (2005) identified liver disease as a major cause of death among HIV-infected patients, emphasizing the role of hepatitis C and B viruses and alcohol, as published in the Journal of Hepatology. 41. Nikolopoulos et al. (2009) conducted a cohort study and meta-analysis on the impact of hepatitis B virus infection on AIDS progression and mortality in HIV-infected individuals, as reported in Clinical Infectious Diseases. 42. Martin-Carbonero et al. (2011) evaluated clinical and virological outcomes in HIV-infected patients with chronic hepatitis B on long-term nucleos(t)ide analogues, as published in AIDS. 43. Matthews et al. (2008) conducted a randomized trial of combination hepatitis B therapy in HIV/HBV co-infected antiretroviral-naïve individuals in Thailand, as reported in Hepatology. 44. Matthews et al. (2009) linked combination HBV therapy to greater HBV DNA suppression in lamivudine-experienced HIV/HBV co-infected individuals, as published in AIDS. 45. Benhamou et al. (1999) studied liver fibrosis progression in HIV and hepatitis C virus co-infected patients, as reported in Hepatology. 46. Deng et al. (2009) conducted a meta-analysis on the impact of HIV infection on the course of hepatitis C virus infection, as published in the World Journal of Gastroenterology. 47. Pineda et al. (2005) found that HIV co-infection shortens the survival of patients with hepatitis C virus-related decompensated cirrhosis, as reported in Hepatology. 48. Thein et al. (2008) analyzed the natural history of hepatitis C virus infection in HIV-infected individuals and the impact of HIV in the HAART era, as published in AIDS. 49. Castel et al. (2012) proposed the use of community viral load as a population-based biomarker of HIV burden, as reported in AIDS. 50. Cowan et al. (2012) observed a stable incidence of HIV diagnoses among Danish MSM despite increased engagement in unsafe sex, as published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes. 51. Das et al. (2010) reported that decreases in community viral load are accompanied by reductions in new HIV infections in San Francisco, as published in PLoS ONE. 52. Fang et al. (2004) observed decreased HIV transmission following a policy of providing free access to HAART in Taiwan, as reported in the Journal of Infectious Diseases. 53. Hogg et al. (2013) noted a HAART-related decrease in the rate of new HIV diagnoses, as presented at the 19th Annual Conference on Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections. 54. Geng et al. (2012) evaluated the effect of a universal antiretroviral therapy recommendation on HIV RNA levels among patients entering care with a CD4 count greater than 500/μL, as published in Clinical Infectious Diseases. 55. Katz et al. (2002) studied the impact of HAART on HIV seroincidence among men who have sex with men in San Francisco, as reported in the American Journal of Public Health. 56. Law et al. (2011) analyzed trends in detectable viral load by calendar year in the Australian HIV observational database, as published in the Journal of the International AIDS Society. 57. Manavi et al. (2013) examined community viral load counts and new HIV-positive patients in Birmingham, United Kingdom, between 2006 and 2011, with findings accessible online. 58. Montaner et al. (2010) associated HAART coverage with decreased HIV/AIDS morbidity and new HIV diagnoses in British Columbia, Canada, as published in The Lancet. 59. Montaner et al. (2013) updated the treatment as prevention experience in British Columbia, Canada, with findings accessible online. 60. Porco et al. (2004) reported a decline in HIV infectivity following the introduction of HAART, as published in AIDS. 61. Wood et al. (2009) analyzed longitudinal community plasma HIV-1 RNA concentrations and HIV-1 incidence among injecting drug users, as reported in the British Medical Journal. 62. The ANRS 12136 TEMPRANO trial evaluated early antiretroviral treatment and/or early isoniazid prophylaxis against tuberculosis in HIV-infected adults, with findings accessible online. 63. The WHO (2010) provided guidelines on the use of antiretroviral drugs for treating pregnant women and preventing HIV infections in infants, emphasizing a public health approach. 64. Schouten et al. (2011) discussed the prevention of mother-to-child transmission of HIV and its alignment with health-related Millennium Development Goals, as published in The Lancet. 65. The CDC (2013) reported on the impact of an innovative approach to prevent mother-to-child transmission of HIV in Malawi, as detailed in the MMWR Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. 66. Taha et al. (2011) updated efficacy results of the PEPIMalawi trial on postexposure prophylaxis of breastfeeding HIV-exposed infants with antiretroviral drugs, as published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes. 67. The Kesho Bora Study Group (2011) compared triple antiretroviral prophylaxis with zidovudine and single-dose nevirapine during pregnancy and breastfeeding for preventing mother-to-child transmission of HIV-1, as published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases. 68. Coovadia et al. (2012) evaluated the efficacy and safety of an extended nevirapine regimen in breastfeeding infants of HIV-1-infected mothers, as reported in The Lancet. 69. Jamieson et al. (2010) studied maternal or infant antiretroviral drugs to reduce HIV-1 transmission, as published in the New England Journal of Medicine. 70. Jamieson et al. (2012) followed up on maternal and infant antiretroviral regimens to prevent postnatal HIV-1 transmission, as reported in The Lancet. 71. The Kesho Bora Study Group (2012) analyzed maternal HIV-1 disease progression 18–24 months post-delivery based on antiretroviral prophylaxis regimens, as published in Clinical Infectious Diseases. 72. Ciaranello et al. (2013) assessed the cost-effectiveness of WHO 2010 guidelines for preventing mother-to-child HIV transmission in Zimbabwe, as reported in Clinical Infectious Diseases. 73. Fasawé et al. (2013) conducted a cost-effectiveness analysis of Option B+ for HIV prevention and treatment of mothers and children in Malawi, as published in PLoS ONE. 74. Nachega et al. (2012) reviewed adherence to ART during and after pregnancy in low-, middle-, and high-income countries, as published in AIDS. 75. Ekouevi et al. (2012) studied maternal CD4+ cell count decline after interruption of antiretroviral prophylaxis for preventing mother-to-child transmission of HIV, as reported in PLoS ONE. 76. The WHO toolkit provided guidance on expanding and simplifying treatment for pregnant women living with HIV, with resources accessible online. 77. The WHO (2010) issued guidelines on HIV and infant feeding, emphasizing principles and recommendations for infant feeding in the context of HIV.
